relationship: Thematic comparison of divine protection of the holy city
rationale: The letter credits God with driving out opponents arrayed against the holy city. The psalm describes God supporting His city while assembled kings are troubled and shaken. Both locate the city's security in God's action against threatening rulers; the psalm is not identified as a prediction or account of this particular expulsion.

relationship: Liturgical parallel of a leader and answering assembly
rationale: Jonathan begins the prayer while the priests and others respond during the sacrifice; Esdras blesses the Lord and all the people answer Amen. Both depict public prayer with a leader and a responding congregation. The occasions remain distinct; Maccabees does not specify an Amen response, and Jonathan is not identified with Esdras.

The priests sing hymns in response after the sacrificial prayer; at the foundation of the Lord's house, priests and Levites participate in answering praise and thanksgiving. The shared practice is responsive temple praise, without identifying the unnamed hymns in Maccabees as Ezra's quoted refrain or equating the ceremonies.

relationship: Archival preservation of royal provisions for sacred gifts
rationale: Nehemiah's reported library includes kings' letters about dedicated gifts. Ezra describes a treasury-library search and a preserved memorandum of Cyrus's provisions for rebuilding the Jerusalem house and returning its gold and silver vessels. Both associate collected written royal records with sacred endowments; Ezra's memorandum is not asserted to be one of Nehemiah's particular letters or in the same archive.

relationship: Literary reflection on the bodily cost of study and writing
rationale: The abridger describes the work of producing the condensed history as sweat and sleeplessness. Ecclesiastes links the making of many books and much study with weariness of the flesh. Both explicitly connect literary work with bodily strain, while the abridger willingly undertakes the task and Ecclesiastes issues a caution.

relationship: Comparison of building metaphors for different responsibilities
rationale: The abridger distinguishes an architect's concern for the whole foundation from the decorator's work to explain historian and abridger roles. Paul distinguishes laying a foundation as a master builder from another person's building upon it. Both use construction roles to distinguish responsibilities; Paul's foundation is explicitly Jesus Christ, and the literary historian is not equated with that foundation.

relationship: Visible facial distress revealing inner sorrow
rationale: Onias's changed face reveals the anguish of his soul to observers. The king reads the speaker's distressed face as distress of heart, and the speaker explains his grief over the devastated city. Both make facial appearance an outward sign of inward sorrow; the threatened temple deposits and the burned city gates are different causes.

People leave their houses for public supplication because the sanctuary is threatened with contempt, while the priests plead in the surrounding scene. Joel calls the congregation together and has the priests ask that God's inheritance not be given to reproach or foreign rule. Both present communal assembly and priestly petition against disgrace, without treating Heliodorus's mission as the fulfilment of Joel's summons.

relationship: Sacrifice and vows after danger to life
rationale: Heliodorus sacrifices and makes vows to the One who preserved his life after his near-fatal ordeal. Jonah recalls his failing life and promises thankful sacrifice and repayment of his vows while praying for deliverance. Both connect endangered life, appeal to the Lord, sacrifice and vows; Heliodorus's enacted offering and Jonah's promised offering remain distinct.

The priests in Maccabees despise the temple and neglect its sacrifices in favour of athletic exercises. Malachi rebukes priests who belittle God's name and treat His table as despised by bringing polluted and defective offerings. Both condemn priests' contempt for their altar responsibilities, with neglect for athletics distinguished from the presentation of unacceptable offerings.

relationship: Royal mourning for a man unjustly killed
rationale: Antiochus weeps over Onias after learning of his unjust murder and admiring his conduct. David leads mourning for Abner, weeps at his grave and laments his fall before men of injustice. Both narratives show a king grieving an unjust killing, without equating the victims, their offices or the kings' later treatment of the killers.

relationship: Loss of mourning and honourable burial
rationale: Jason, who left others unburied, receives neither mourning nor funeral care or an ancestral tomb. Jeremiah announces that Jehoiakim will not be mourned and will receive a dishonourable burial outside Jerusalem's gate. Both portray deprivation of mourning and proper burial as an ignominious end, without identifying Jason with Jehoiakim or assigning the same disposal of the body to both.

relationship: Comparison of lists describing slaughter across age and sex
rationale: The massacre narrative lists young and old, women, children, virgins and infants among those killed. Ezekiel's vision similarly lists old men, young men, maidens, infants and women in the order to strike Jerusalem. The shared enumeration conveys the breadth of the killing; the vision explicitly exempts those bearing the sign, and Antiochus's soldiers are not identified with its agents or granted its divine commission.

relationship: Wisdom principle linking honourable age and righteousness
rationale: Eleazar judges his resolve by the dignity of old age and his lifelong excellent conduct, with God's law foremost. Proverbs calls old age a crown of boasting found in ways of righteousness. The narrative embodies the connection between honourable age and righteous conduct; the proverb does not name Eleazar or prescribe his particular martyrdom.

relationship: Wisdom principle of conduct fitting gray hair
rationale: Eleazar's resolve is described as worthy of his age and distinguished gray hair alongside his excellent conduct from childhood. Sirach calls judgment, wisdom and counsel fitting for gray hair and elders, and names fear of the Lord their boast. Both link the honour of age to moral and discerning conduct, without claiming Sirach describes Eleazar's biography or commands his particular decision.
